rationale: Mara Voss built silhouette-first: five big masses (head, pauldron slab, coat, med-gun, boots) and nothing else. Head is rows 2-16 (15px) against a 61px figure - ~3.8 heads, cartoon-heavy. The one deliberate composition move is the oversized med-gun held level at the hip: a 12px-wide horizontal bar jutting fully clear of the left edge, the only horizontal in an otherwise all-vertical figure, so the outline has a landmark you can name from across the room. Balanced by an equally oversized bare fist low-right and a splayed 5px-crotch boot stance. Internal detail is rationed to five things that each do a job: visor, bone cross on the rust chest plate, belt, rust armband on one pauldron only (asymmetry), respirator grille. This revision is a rendering and palette pass, not a redraw. Not one pixel of the silhouette, the pose or the ink contour moved: the alpha mask and every #120b10 ink position are bit-identical to the previous draft (1727 opaque, 1345 clear, verified pixel-for-pixel against it). What changed is that 24 colours became 58, and the figure stopped reading as flat colour fields. Every material now carries a ramp instead of two flats - 9 steps for the coat, 9 for the helmet shell, 7 for boot leather, 6 each for rust livery, gunmetal and trousers, 4 each for skin, bone and visor glass, plus 3 inks. Each ramp shifts hue as it descends rather than running a pure value gradient: lights go warm (coat #9ba09b, rust #eeb184, skin #d49a78, helmet #c6b8b4) and shadows go cool and blue-violet (coat #1a2029, rust #45201e, skin #4a3130, helmet #1f1a28), so a form turns by temperature as much as by brightness and the cold grey-plum of the coat still reads against the rust. Shading is driven off the geometry rather than hand-placed blobs, which is what keeps it consistent with the rest of the set. The load-bearing rule: a plane break with open sky beyond it is a top plane and catches the upper-left key, but a break with more sprite beyond it is an overhang and takes a cast shadow instead. Collapsing those two cases into one is exactly what made the first attempt read flat; separating them is what put shadow under the pauldron slab, under the belt, under the chest plate and under the jaw. A hardness rank then decides seams: where a harder material lies over a softer one - belt over coat, rust plate over coat, bone cross over plate - the top edge is proud of the surface and takes a lit lip rather than a shadow, so material transitions are visible at every seam. Convex upper-left contours pick up a rim light along the ink, giving hard corners their glint. Vertical fold streaks on an irregular 11px period give the coat and trousers the weight of hanging cloth; boots get the creases only, never the highlight. Grime is low-frequency blob noise that thickens below row 44 so the hem and boots are the filthiest part of her, with sparse one-step scuffs bitten out of rust, gunmetal, leather and bone. Guards, because a shading engine will happily smear a load-bearing read into mush: bone and skin are locked to a narrow band of their ramps so the medic cross and the face never blow out or go muddy; regions under 24px get a top lip and a bottom shadow only, with no side terms, which is what saved the bone cross and the armband; the gun sight sits one step down so it cannot outshout the pauldron armband; and the visor is shaded by row and source value alone, so the paired speculars stay bit-identical to each other. Across rows 13-20 mirrored pixels of the same material are clamped to within one ramp step, so upper-left light tilts the face without breaking its bilateral read. #120b10 is still the deepest ink anchor and still wraps the whole silhouette as one continuous contour - nothing in the 58-colour legend is darker than it. No magenta, no chartreuse. Transparency is real: space maps to RGBA 0,0,0,0, no background is baked in, and no interior pixel carries the transparent value. Sacrifices unchanged from the first pass: zero facial nuance (she is a helmet and a mouth grille), and the arms are still welded into the shoulder slab, so this wants whole-body squash/bob rather than an IK rig.
frontFacingCue: A 22px-wide visor band split by a 2px plum-black nose bridge into two lenses, each carrying an identical 3px specular at the same relative position within its lens - paired highlights read as eyes and only work head-on. It is still the brightest value on the sprite (#f0fdf4 peak over #a8dcd4 glass) sitting directly against a hard ink frame above and below, so the contrast survives any downscale. The repaint deliberately does not light the glass from the upper-left the way the rest of the figure is lit: the visor is shaded by row alone, so identical source glass in the same row resolves to exactly the same colour on both lenses and the pass cannot introduce any new asymmetry into the cue. Below it, three cues stack, all bilaterally paired about column 23.5: an exposed skin band across the cheeks, a centred dark respirator grille with a lit metal lip, and cheek guards in helmet-shadow value dropping back on both sides. Upper-left light does tilt the lower face, but mirrored pixels are held to within one ramp step of each other so the pairing still reads. The head is also pushed clear of the shoulder line - jaw ends row 16, four rows of 6px neck with open transparent air on both sides, shoulders do not start until row 21 - so the down-angle cannot swallow it, and nothing rises above the shoulder line to compete.
smallCheck: Re-checked after the repaint by box-filtering to 21x28 and looking at it. It survives, and the extra values help more than they hurt. The head stays a distinct block clear of the shoulders, the visor collapses to a single bright horizontal dash that still reads as a face, the bone cross survives as a legible pale plus, the crotch gap keeps the legs separate, and the gun remains a recognisable mass sticking out to the left. Two things the palette pass actually improved at size: the pauldron slab now separates from the torso because its top plane is lit and the chest beneath it is in cast shadow, where before both averaged to the same grey; and the boots now separate from the trousers on value rather than relying on the ink line, which was the first thing to go when the ink got averaged away. What is still lost: weapon internals blur into one grey-and-rust smudge, so it reads as "she is holding something big" rather than "med-gun"; the belt buckle and knuckle catch-lights vanish; the respirator merges with the jaw shadow into a single dark mouth blob; and the fold streaks and grime average out entirely below about 34px, which is correct - they are texture for the large size and they degrade to the flat mid-tone they were sampled around rather than to noise. Nothing turns into visual noise, which is the real test. If ~28px is the shipping size I would still bump the visor to 4 rows and drop the armband.
